# Probe: build the static numerals for real

The design has a name: **the static numerals**. The numeral types exist at compile time only, with the four numbers as static parameters. Batch 29 built another design, **the field numerals**: run-time value objects with the four numbers as fields and getters. Use these two names in your report.

You build a prototype of the curator's design for numerals in the Fortress revival, `/home/user/fortress`, in a worktree of your own, on both paths, and you measure what it costs. You build; you do not cost by reading. Load the `fortress-repo` skill first, read its `references/revival-changes.md` whole, and the parts your work needs (`build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `toolchain.md`, `interpreter.md`, `compiler.md`, `library.md`, `specification.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md`, `gate.md`, `records.md`, `exploring.md`, `committing.md`). You are exploring: you commit your report and your patch, never the code.

## The design, and its one source

The design is section 3 of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md`, confirmed by the curator in his words; sections 4 and 11 give what it is not and the consequences he confirmed; section 6 his words with their transcript lines. Read sections 2, 3, 4, 6 and 11 whole before anything else. The Working Draft's own text is `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-175`; read it at the source.

Take no design from P-174, the held list, `CLIMB-BATCH-29.md`, `climb-batch-29-review.md` or `explorations/reviews/numeral-fidelity-2026-11-09.md`: each carries the words "fields of the value, not static parameters", which the snapshot's section 7 traces to the coordinator, not to the curator. Read them only for what batch 29 built (`numeral-fidelity-2026-11-09.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-29-review.md`) and for the record's measured facts.

In one paragraph: a numeral has a type at compile time only, the Draft's `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` below `Numeral`, with the four numbers (digit count `n`, digits after the point `m`, radix `r`, the digits as one integer `v`) as static parameters, so `3.125` has the type `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Where a type is fixed, the compiler converts at compile time from the exact value: exactly into the integer types and `QQ`, with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`, a refusal at compile time when the value does not fit. A number type, the library's own as much as a program's, takes a numeral by declaring a coercion generic over the four numbers, whose body is a call of the type's constructor on values computed from `n, m, r, v`; the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and emits the constructor call with the constants, once per place, into a `static final` field that the class's initializer fills; for a built-in type that call folds to a JVM constant. Where nothing fixes a type, the machine default (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by size; `RR64`), then the same conversion. An expression of numerals alone folds exactly first; a numeral has no sign, so `-3` at a program's type is the type's own `-` applied to the coercion's result, both once at load. No numeral object exists at run time: no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString`, no `=` pairs on a numeral type. Walk does the same thing at the first evaluation of each place, fixing the coercion's static arguments from the numeral's four numbers. `nat` is unbounded in the type system; the 32-bit `nat` is this implementation's array-size choice.

## What to build, in order, measuring after each step

1. **The base build** at `main`'s head, as `/home/user/fortress-base30`, by `references/worktrees.md`, in the background with a log; then your worktree `/home/user/fortress-proto-draft` seeded from it. Read the disk first (`df -P /home/user`); stop if either would leave under 14 G.
2. **The one library.** Replace batch 29's two value objects (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:454-494` and their `.fss` bodies: the four getters, `asString`, `asFloat`, the 22 `=` pairs) with the Draft's types as static-parameter types below `Numeral`, and give `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` their coercions in the generic form. The Draft leaves the hierarchy undescribed (its note at `literals.tex:93-99`); choose the simplest that works and report it as a decision not taken.
3. **The checker.** A numeral's type with its four static arguments, `v` beyond 32 bits; inference of a generic coercion's static arguments from the numeral's type; the range refusal as a static error; P-173's default where nothing fixes a type, kept as it is. Run the count stage and the distance stage on the one library and the checker's timing check (`references/compiler.md`, `references/gate.md`) before and after.
4. **The code generator and the runtime.** At a built-in target, the fold to a JVM constant (batch 29's fold, kept, with `-3` and `-2147483648` folded exactly first). At a program's type, the generic coercion instantiated at the numeral's static arguments, the constructor call once per place into a `static final`, the type's `-` applied after it for a negative constant; `v` beyond 32 bits in the class loader's stamped constants (`RTTIsize.of` holds an `int` today). The design wants no class per numeral: the compiled path specializes a generic by a class per instantiation, so do not let each numeral site make one; compile the coercion as one method that takes the four numbers as values and have the static initializer call it with the constants, or inline the body at the site, and report which you did and why. The compiler's prelude carries the same declarations, so that compiled programs run on them before the switch-over: the curator made the exception to P-37 for the numerals at 17:1x UTC on 11-09 ("Of course, I'm making exception for the P37."); the prelude's copy goes with the prelude at the switch-over. So the prelude's `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` go too, and the compiled tests that write `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` are rewritten.
5. **Walk.** The numeral converted at a fixed place from the four numbers, once, at the first evaluation; the default elsewhere; at a program's type the generic coercion instantiated with the four numbers as static arguments and run once per place; `-3` as the type's `-` after it; no `Numerals.object`, no run-time numeral value. Row 486, a `nat` static parameter used as a value under walk, stands in the way: fix it or find walk's way around it, and report which.
6. **The tests**, written first, each seen failing through the harness, then passing, on both paths where the path can run it. Batch 29 left tests in the field numerals' form: `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss` holds `CC64`, the interval `Iv`, `Dec`, a round trip `Written` and the radix cases, each written against the getters and `asFloat` (`coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) = CC64(asFloat(x), 0.0)`; `Dec(x.digitValue, x.fractionDigits)`; `Written(x.asString)`), and the compiled tests under `compiler_tests/Numeral*` and `LiteralDefault*` write `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` against the prelude. 7. **The gate's stages** that your tree can run: the compiled suites, the walk suite once at the end, the count, the distance, the checker's timing. Report each flip by name and line, with the team tests that change.

# The static numerals, built: a prototype on both paths

The design is the curator's, the static numerals: section 3 of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md`, with sections 4 and 11. Batch 29 built another design, the field numerals: run-time value objects with the four numbers as fields and getters (`explorations/reviews/numeral-fidelity-2026-11-09.md`, section 2). This probe builds the static numerals in a worktree, on both paths, and measures what they cost. Nothing here weighs one design against the other.

- Base: `dd00743d9e`, `main`'s head when the probe started. Base build: `/home/user/fortress-base30`, built in place by `references/worktrees.md`. Worktree: `/home/user/fortress-proto-draft`, detached, seeded from it ("seeded from /home/user/fortress-base30 (dd00743d9e) in 3 s"). The worktree is removed at the end; its whole change is `draft-numerals.patch`, `git diff dd00743d9e` with the new files added by `git add -N`.
- Machine: `nproc` 4, Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 2100 MHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`; load at the first count 0.35, 0.57, 0.27 (`uptime`).
- Disk before the base build: `df -P /home/user` printed 20617500 1K-blocks available; after seeding, 20031136. A built tree is about 1.5 GB (`du -sh --exclude=.git /home/user/fortress`), so both trees left more than 14 G.
- Citations of the tree are at `dd00743d9e` unless they name the patch; the patch's code is cited by file and method, since the worktree is gone.

## 1. Where the snapshot and the record differ

The probe followed the snapshot in each case.

- P-173 says a place fixes a type when its declared type "is a numeral type". The snapshot's point 1 and section 4 give a numeral type no value at run time, and P-174 says a numeral type is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. Built: a binding at a numeral type is refused on both paths (`tests/NumeralTypeNoValueWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/LiteralTypeUnwritable.fss`).
- A static expression at a program's own type: the snapshot's section 11 says in one bullet "only through a coercion from `ZZ32` or `QQ`" and in its last bullet "through a coercion from `QQ` or `ZZ`"; P-174 says "through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`". Built: through the coercion from the folded value's default type, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, `QQ` for a quotient, `RR64` with a radix point.
- Row 486, which the brief and the snapshot's section 11 name as standing in walk's way, is `FIXED` (`53a6074ed`) and is about the compiled checker. Walk reads a `nat` used as a value already, as a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` from 2^31 (F-140). What stood in walk's way was elsewhere (section 6).
- The snapshot's section 2 quotes the Draft's `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` with three static parameters and `RadixPointNumeral[\n,m,10,v\]` with four; P-174 gives the four numbers to both. Built: the Draft's arities, `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` and `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`; a coercion from a natural numeral reads `m` as 0 by not having it.

## 2. Step 1: the base build

- Commands, from `references/worktrees.md`: `git worktree add --detach /home/user/fortress-base30 dd00743d9e`, then in it `ant compileAll`, the library order and `bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, in the background with a log. Output: "BUILD SUCCESSFUL / Total time: 47 seconds / EXIT=0", and the five jars `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar`, `CompilerSystem.jar`; `git status --porcelain` printed nothing.
- `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh /home/user/fortress-base30 /home/user/fortress-proto-draft - dd00743d9e`.
- The base's checker, timed by `references/compiler.md`, "The checker's time": `time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out> <scratch>`, run from the base build: "#total 0 / #locations 0 / #crash none", "real 1m44.733s".
- The base's distance stage, `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out> <scratch>`, from the base build: "#total 0 / #crash none / #seconds 161 FortressLibrary 102".

## 3. Step 2: the one library

What was built (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `.fss`; `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi`, `.fss`):

- The field numerals' two value objects, with their four getters, `asString`, `asFloat` and the 22 `=` pairs, are gone, with the two private helpers only `asString` used (`numeralDigits`, `numeralSuffix`). The `^` overloads on a numeral exponent (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`) are gone too: a numeral exponent converts at `^`'s other declarations.
- In their place, five traits with no members:

      trait Numeral extends Number end
      trait AnyNaturalNumeral extends Numeral excludes { AnyRadixPointNumeral } end
      trait AnyRadixPointNumeral extends Numeral end
      trait NaturalNumeral[\nat n, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyNaturalNumeral end
      trait RadixPointNumeral[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyRadixPointNumeral end

  The two `Any` traits exist only so that a type's coercion from each numeral type overloads with the other: two instantiations of different generic traits do not exclude each other otherwise. The library's own way for this is `AnyIntegral` above `Integral[\I\]`.
- Each of the eight number types takes a numeral by a coercion generic over the four numbers, whose body computes the value from them, as `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = v.asZZ32` at `ZZ32`, `= Ratio(v, 1)` and `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = v / r^(m.asZZ32)` at `QQ`, and `= numeralRR64(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32)` at `RR64`, the library's one-rounding helper. `AnyIntegral`'s coercion chooses `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` from `v`.
- Lines: `git diff dd00743d9e --shortstat` over the four files: "4 files changed, 42 insertions(+), 145 deletions(-)".

Measured after this step, with the base's checker:

- Count stage: no total. "checker-count: the run printed no error total (rc=1)"; its output, `ClassCastException: class scala.runtime.BoxedUnit cannot be cast to class com.sun.fortress.nodes.IntExpr`, from `STypesUtil$outFinder` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:2151-2159`): the base checker types a numeral by the plain `NaturalNumeral`, cannot infer a generic coercion's sizes from it, leaves a size inference variable in the checked library, and the post-check walker returns `Unit` at an `IntExpr` position instead of reporting it. Row 291 holds the same crash from another trigger; its notes have 29 characters left, so this trigger is here only.
- Distance stage: "#total 8", one or two in each of six components, and six crash rows, each that `ClassCastException`.

## 4. Step 3: the checker

What was built:

- A numeral's type carries its four numbers as static arguments, `v` at any size: `3.125` is `RadixPointNumeral[\4,3,10,3125\]`, `3000000000` is `NaturalNumeral[\10,10,3000000000\]` (`impls/Misc.scala`, the literal cases; `compiler/Types.java`, `numeralType`). The four numbers come from one new helper that both paths and the code generator use, `nodes_util/NumeralNumbers.java`, a port of batch 29's reading in `Numerals.java`. The analyzer compares sizes by their `BigInteger` values already (`scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:120-131`), so `v` beyond 32 bits needed no change there. The kind check refused it: "Ill-formed static argument: 9223372036854775807", eight errors in five places; a numeral type's arguments and a numeral coercion's static arguments are now exempt (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`).
- Inference of a generic coercion's static arguments from the numeral's type is the checker's own static-argument inference (`CoercionOracle.checkCoercionTrait`, `inferStaticParams`); it worked unchanged. `getCoercionTargetsFrom`, which skipped every generic coercion, now admits one generic over a numeral's four numbers (`CoercionOracle.scala`), so a numeral still promotes a generic call (P-74).
- The range refusal as a static error: a coercion's `where` clause of size comparisons, as `where { v < 256 }`, is computed exactly at the inferred four numbers; a coercion whose clause fails is not a candidate, and the refusal reads "The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte." (`CoercionOracle.whereHolds`, `numeralRefusal`). Only comparisons of sizes are read; any other constraint is left to the checks that read it. At the eight library types the range refusal is batch 29's, by the value (`NumeralConversion.outOfRange`), not by a `where` clause (section 12, decision 6).
- Inside a coercion over a numeral type, the four numbers read as values are `ZZ`, exact integers; elsewhere a `nat` read as a value stays a `ZZ32` (P-173): `KindEnv.getType` and `markExact`, set from the declaration's parameter type in `impls/Decls.scala`.
- A numeral has no sign. The fold (`compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java`) now marks its results by their text: prefix minus on a numeral as written keeps the written text after `-`, any other folded constant is written in parentheses, `(5)`. A radix-point numeral under a minus is folded the same way, its node holding the magnitude so that `-0.0` keeps its sign where it converts. At a library type the signed value converts directly, as before, so `-2147483648` at `ZZ32` folds exactly first. At a program's own type a negative constant is the type's own prefix minus on the coercion of the numeral as written: the checker checks that minus on a stand-in of the type and puts the coercion in its place (`STypeChecker.scala`, `coercions.negator`), with the component's own disambiguated prefix minus, which the fold now records per component (`prefixMinusOf`). A type without a prefix minus refuses it: "The numeral -3 at Plain needs a prefix minus on Plain, which it does not declare." Any other folded constant reaches a program's type only through its default's type (`CoercionOracle.buildCoercion`; `defaultFits` does the rest).
- P-173's default where nothing fixes a type is kept as it is. Two places changed because two numerals now have two types: an `if`, `case`, `try` or block whose results are numerals, alone or beside values that already fit, converts each numeral branch at the expected type in place (`numeralJoinInto`, `joinInto`, the `if`'s winning-clause path in `impls/Misc.scala`), and a tuple of numerals converts element by element in place (`buildCoercion`). Before, the checker coerced such a join or tuple as a whole, which ran a numeral's coercion at run time on an `IntLiteral` value; the static numerals have no value to run it on.
- Lines: `scala_src` and `compiler/Types.java`, "8 files changed, 316 insertions(+), 32 deletions(-)"; the fold and `NumeralNumbers.java`, "2 files changed, 161 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)".

Measured (count and distance stages over the one library, timed by `references/compiler.md`): the first run after the change, "#total 9 / #locations 5" (1m10.783s), the eight kind errors and one tuple join; then "#total 0 / #locations 0 / #crash none", "real 1m43.093s". The final runs are in section 8.

## 5. Step 4: the code generator, the runtime and the prelude

What was built:

- At a built-in target, batch 29's fold to a JVM constant is kept: the coercion desugarer retypes the numeral at the library type and the code generator emits the constant (`CoercionDesugarer.foldsTo`; `CodeGen.forIntLiteralExpr`, `forFloatLiteralExpr`). The checker now finds that coercion through the library's generic coercion, so the type check of the conversion is the common mechanism; the fold itself is recognised by the target type, not by evaluating the coercion's body (decision 3). A negated radix-point numeral is negated after its one rounding, so `-0.0` is IEEE's negative zero.
- At a program's own type, the coercion generic over the four numbers is inlined at its site: the code generator takes the lifted coercion's body from the component, replaces each of the four numbers read as a value by its constant, a `ZZ`, and each static parameter of the coercion's type by the site's static argument, and compiles the body in the component class's static initializer into a `static final` field that the site reads (`CodeGen.inlinedNumeralCoercion`, `numeralCoercionDecl`, `emitNumeralCoercionSites`). No class is made per numeral, and the class loader stamps nothing for `v`, so `RTTIsize.of`'s `int` does not stand in the way of a 20-digit `v`. Why inlining and not one method that takes the four numbers as values: the body is already typed with the four numbers as `ZZ` values, so substituting constants needs no new method, signature or call; and a coercion of a generic type, `Gen[\T\]`, takes its type argument by the same substitution (`StaticTypeReplacer`, keeping the callee references' own generic schemas). Its limit: the coercion must be declared in the same component (section 10).
- A site at a program's generic type is now hoisted too, where its type names no type variable: `site(): Gen[\RR64\] = 3` gives one object per place (row 957's case; `numeralCoercionSiteDesc`).
- `-3` at a program's type compiles as the type's `-` on the hoisted coercion; the minus itself runs at each evaluation (section 10).
- The prelude (P-37's exception for the numerals, his words at 17:1x UTC on 11-09): the same five traits, `Numeral extends Number` with an `excludes` list of the prelude's number types, since they have no `comprises` clauses; the coercions of `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ32`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR64` and `RR32` in the generic form, their bodies through the prelude's own helpers (`bigOverflowingToLong`, `numeralToDouble`, `numeralToFloat`). `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` are gone, with the `simpleIntLiteralArith` import. The prelude's own code wrote getters on numerals, `(1).asZZ` and `(1).asNN32` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:561-570`, `:814`, `:816`, `:750`, `:752`); they are respelled with the prelude's helpers or a typed binding.
- The runtime: a size read as a value no longer goes through an `IntLiteral`. The class loader stamps it as a `ZZ32`, `FZZ32.make`, or for a size beyond `ZZ32` `FZZ32.makeSize`, which raises the error of row 962 as before (`runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java`, `natMethod`; `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java`), and the code generator reads it without `asZZ32` (`CodeGen.forVarRef`). A numeral that no place typed compiles as its default constant, not as an `IntLiteral` (`forIntLiteralExpr`). `nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java` loses its two literal branches.
- Lines: code generator "1 file changed, 118 insertions(+), 40 deletions(-)"; runtime "3 files changed, 16 insertions(+), 22 deletions(-)"; prelude "2 files changed, 51 insertions(+), 130 deletions(-)".

What stood in the way, and how it was passed:

- The prelude's overloading check refused each type's two coercions, `[\nat n, nat r, nat v\]NaturalNumeral[\n,r,v\]->ZZ` beside `ZZ32->ZZ` ("Invalid overloading of coerce_ZZ in API CompilerBuiltin"): its number traits do not exclude a trait. The `excludes` list settled it.
- Every compiled program died at the prelude's own static initializer, `NoClassDefFoundError: CompilerBuiltin` (`fortress run hello`): a component with a generic overloaded top-level function stores its inference cache tables into a class named without its package (`CodeGen.java:1979`). The prelude's coercions are the first such functions in a library component. Fixed in the patch; filed as row 972.
- A coercion body that spawns, as `digitsOf(...) || hexDigit(...)`, fails the class's load: the static initializer runs on the main thread before the task pool (`MainWrapper.java:61-63`), `ClassCastException: Thread cannot be cast to FortressTaskRunner`. Batch 29's hoisted sites fail the same way on the base (probe below). Not fixed; the test binds its operands first; filed as row 971.

content.content:
## Judge and repair round

A judge runs on a rung only on a contested fix, a refusal or a worker's stop, and on the merged tree only on a blocking review or a red gate. It builds and tests nothing. It writes `JUDGE.md` (on the rung's branch, or `JUDGE-<kind>.md` in the batch's folder) and commits it.

- On contested fixes it rules on each listed fix alone: uphold, or revert it itself with `git revert --no-edit`, which takes the fix's test with it. Its decision is `stands`, `repair` (numbered instructions for one round), `drop` or `stop`.
- On a refusal, the same four.
- On a stop, `repair` means the stop is not one: the worker resumes and its skeptic follows. Any other decision leaves the rung stopped.

Its brief carries its question, the contested fixes with both arguments, and the worker's decisions. It points to the checks slice, each fix's commit and the sections of `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` it needs. In batch 10 a judge's brief carried the worker's whole result and the skeptic's verdict, two thirds of its 61K tokens, and the judge used about 30% of them (`process-engineering/checking-roles-cost.md`, section 2).

A first ruling on a rung or the merged tree runs on Opus; a second on the same one on Fable (`judgeTier`; the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The roles", and `references/delegating.md`, "Which tier runs what").

A repair round is the rung worker again, with the checks slice, the judge's decision and the rung's section. It carries out the instructions in order, test first, and updates `REPORT.md` and `record.md`, whose texts replace the worker's; its structured result replaces the worker's too, so it describes the whole rung as it now stands. No skeptic follows it: its own test, the review and the gate check it. A repair that does not land drops the rung. No second repair round is taken.

## Gather

The gather composes one local commit per approved rung on `main`; nothing is merged.

- **The order.** First, a rung goes after every rung it lands only with (`landsOnlyWith`), so that no commit on `main` holds a rung without the rungs it needs: in climb batch 17 the old rule, which compared lines across files, put rung L's `2b1cd8e63` before rung W's `743eb5286`, and that commit alone fails `LibraryOverloadFamilies.fss:37` (`reviews/batch-17-review.md`, finding 2). Then the rungs that share a file go in the ascending order of their lowest edited line in that file, so that a later hunk does not shift lines a landed record cites; a line is compared only with a line of the same file, and rungs that share no file keep the manifest's order. Where two files order one pair both ways, the pair keeps the manifest's order. Any `file:line` a record cites that an earlier hunk shifted is re-anchored by symbol. Tests cite the specification by section, never by line, so no test is re-anchored.
- **Each rung.** Its net diff is applied with `git apply --3way --index`. A conflict in unrelated regions is resolved by hand; one in the same logic is returned, not guessed. Its files are written from the journal where the branch lacks them, by the commands the brief renders per rung. For a repaired rung, `REPORT.md` and `record.md` are always rewritten from the repair round's texts.
- **The record folded.** The FACTS entry under its area. A ledger note that adds a fact through `ledger.py note`. A change to what a row says (its claim narrowed, a half fixed, its test promoted or renamed, its notes at the limit) through `ledger.py rewrite N FILE`: the whole line, stating the gap as it stands now, not its repair history. A note refused for length goes in so, with the notes cut back; none is left out. New rows through `ledger.py add FILE --section TITLE`, each `NEW-<rung>-<n>` placeholder replaced with its number everywhere the rung's files and tests cite it, before the rung's commit. The handover line, in the batch's `RECORD.md`, "Handover lines" (the old handover file is retired into PLAN's first section, which the coordinator keeps). The rung's "Revival change" section is folded into no file: both its parts are copied, word for word, into the batch's `RECORD.md` (below), and nothing is written under `.claude/`. Through batch 13 the gather folded each entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md` as the rung wrote it, and the cold reader that followed made a question's handle findable instead of deleting it: that is how the coordinator's agenda reached the skill (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there").
- **Corrections still owed.** The skeptic's `leftForGather` items. Each sentence of the specification a rung lists as made false and did not edit, corrected to what the code does, each clause checked against its code line. Batch 8's gather saw rung Q's Appendix I Effect false and let it stand, and in batch 9 no stage saw the one rung K made false. Each took a review judge and a repair, 0.53M and 0.39M (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 5; `reviews/batch-9-review.md`, section 6).
- **Text mismatches.** A text mismatch the decisions do not settle is filed, not blocking ("Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect", item 4).
- **Items for the curator.** The gather puts every item a rung, skeptic or judge returned into `PLAN.md`, under "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed" when work waits on it, else under "Off the path, parked".
- **After the rungs.** The landed rungs' walk tests run on the merged tree in one `harness-one.sh` call, each `X.test` named beside its `X.fss`: climb batch 26's gather ran its 20 twice, the first call without the five `.test` files (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 7). One commit closes each row a landed rung fixed (`ledger.py close N --commit HASH --test NAME`, then `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, which fails on any finding, also one the base already had; each is cleared through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or the entry reworded, before the commit). A row whose test is the checker count or the distance stage closes on the rung's run of it, the gate's tables its check: the gather runs neither stage. In climb batch 25 it ran the distance stage for row 873 on code the gate measured again (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 6). One commit writes the batch's `RECORD.md`, once, last: the order and why, each rung's commit, the rows opened and closed, each skeptic's fixes and the contested rulings by commit, the rungs that did not land, the points to report, where each item for the curator went, and last, under "Revival changes, for the skill writer", each landed rung's "Revival change" section, both parts word for word.
- **The specification's PDF.** When the gather builds the specification to check its text, it builds it once, on the text after the last edit under `Specification/`, and keeps the PDF at `tmp/gather/fortress-batch-<N>.pdf` in the main tree, which the commit stage takes ("Commit, and the push held", step 1).

A rung that did not land has its `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` taken out of its branch path by path, its findings folded under "Not landed", and its new rows added. None of its source is applied.

Files are staged by an explicit list and `git diff --cached --stat` is read before each commit. A commit touching a path outside `explorations/` and `.claude/` carries a `historical:` line.

## Review beside the gate

The review and the gate start together on the gather's commits. The review reads and never builds; the gate builds and never reads the record; the gate commits nothing, so the two never commit at once. Run side by side they took 14.7 minutes per batch off the serial tail. The review stays, once (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). Its six checks:

1. Overlaps between rungs, and what their changes do together.
2. Each skeptic's fix and each repair commit, as applied: it does what its finding says, its test seen failing on the worker's head and then passing in its maker's transcript, a settled fix's citation, a reverted fix gone.
3. The folded record: FACTS lines, `ledger.py landing-check BASE` with no finding, also none the base already had, each fixed in the review's corrections commit, no `NEW-` placeholder left where a row is cited, every closed row fixed, the handover, the revival-change material in `RECORD.md` true of the landed code.
4. Each specification sentence a rung listed as made false, corrected.
5. The points to report, with `holdsPush`, and `cannotBeUndone` for a point that holds ("Commit, and the push held").
6. The items for the curator, in `PLAN.md`.

What it does with a finding:

- A record-only or mechanical defect it fixes itself, inside `explorations/`, in one commit.
- A finding settled by tests and records only it routes to the next batch, as `review-routed.N` in `PLAN.md`, with no judge.
- A finding whose repair touches source, library, checker, interpreter or specification goes to a judge, who rules `land`, `repair`, `drop` or `stop`. `land` is for a ruling settled by tests and records after all: its steps go to the next batch and no repair runs.

The review returns its heads before and after its corrections and every path outside `explorations/` they changed. A path the gate reads makes the gate beside it stale, and the gate runs again. Any other path is recorded beside the gate's summary.

A review that returns nothing after three attempts holds nothing: the batch lands on its gate, and `review-missing.1` is listed.

### A review that still blocks after its repair

There is one judge and one repair for the review, and no second review. When the review's repair returns nothing, stops or does not land, the code findings the judge upheld are listed as `review-unrepaired.N` for the next batch. They do not hold the push (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). A step that cannot be undone that the repair reports holds it, as a rung's does.

### A repair of tests and records only

After a repair on the merged tree, the review's or the gate's, the whole gate runs again only when the repair, or the review's corrections, changed a path the gate reads that is not a test file: under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or `build.xml` (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs", and `fortress-repo`'s `references/gate.md`, "When to run it"). In batch 8 the gate ran a second time after a repair of one sentence of Appendix I, 24 minutes on the critical path, with tables identical but for timing (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 4).

A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory.

- The repair returns its heads and changed paths. In `testRuns` it lists each test file it added or changed, run in the harness on the merged tree: the files of one corpus together in one JVM (`ONE_JVM=1 junit.sh`, and one `harness-one.sh` call for the interpreter tests).
- The gate runs again on a code path, a changed test no passing run exercises, a run that failed, or a repair that listed nothing.
- After the gate's repair it also runs again unless every red line is answered by a passing run (`failingAnswered`) and no suite count fell.
- When a red gate stood beside the review, and the review's repair of tests only answers its lines, no gate judge or gate repair runs.
- When the first gate's tables stand, the commit stage appends the runs to `summary.txt` as `# repair-tests` lines, and the paths no stage reads as `# repair-ungated` lines. `gate_compare` skips `#` lines.

`repairRerun` in the script decides.

## Gate

One run on the merged tree, its logs under `tmp/gate-batch-<N>/`, its three outputs written by fixed functions, never by hand. The functions of steps 5 and 7 (`gate_summary`, `gate_compare`, `last_landed_summary`, `ladder_filter`, `ladder_compare`, `mg_phases`) are in `tools/gate-functions.sh`, which the gate sources from the tree's root with `FORTRESS_HOME` set; until 2026-10-10 they were strings of the script (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, finding GA2). Its steps:

1. The disk.
2. `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`, then `ant compileAll`, and at once the distance stage started in the background.
3. The library order if the build started the caches again, then two copies of the caches for the ladder.
4. `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, never both at once, at four threads, pinned in `build.xml` (P-125, "The suites run Fortress in parallel."). Then `ant testSpecData` once an approved rung brings it into the gate, or the last landed summary has a `specdata/` row; every example must pass (P-124, "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.").
5. `summary.txt` from `gate_summary`, one row per suite read from the plain-formatter files under `TEST-RESULTS/`, because the parallel tracks interleave their lines in the ant log. It ends with the `BUILD` and `Total time` lines and the machine it ran on (`# machine `, from `rung-flat-tower/machine.sh`), so that timings are read against their machine. The functions are sourced in a call set up whole, its `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` among it: climb batch 26's gate set `FORTRESS_HOME` alone, and its machine lines hold the proxy's 'Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS' line in place of the JDK's and `FORTRESS_THREADS=unset` (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 3). `gate_compare` against the newest landed summary: a failure, an empty suite, a count that fell or a suite gone is red. The `system-<i>` shards are compared by their sum, since `testSystem` is one suite sharded by sorted index and a new file moves every later file along the shards; climb batch 2's gate went red on exactly that (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md`).
6. The four-thread atomic runs: 14 programs, three runs each, 42 lines. A FAIL, NO-PASS or compile failure is red; a timeout is re-run once.
7. The ladder regression (the skill's `gate.md`): the 85 files of the baseline's pass list compared on phase and output, the `Operation took` line masked, and the eighteen microGPT components compiled only. A DOWN, STDOUT or MISSING line is red unless a rung declared it.
8. The checker count, and 9. the distance, below.

A red gate goes to a judge, then one repair, then one more gate. A gate red after its repair stops the batch, nothing pushed.

### The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage

content.content:
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

Every numeral has the type \TYP{Numeral}, which extends \TYP{Number}, through
one of the two types that \TYP{Numeral} comprises:
a numeral containing only digits has type \TYP{NaturalNumeral},
and a numeral containing a radix point has type \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}.
The value of a numeral holds four numbers:
the number $n$ of its digits, leading zeros among them;
the number $m$ of its digits after the radix point, which is $0$ for a
\TYP{NaturalNumeral};
its radix $r$;
and $v$, the value of its digits, with the radix point deleted, interpreted in
radix $r$.
\Library\ declare these numbers as the getters \VAR{digits},
\VAR{fractionDigits}, \VAR{radix} and \VAR{digitValue} of \TYP{Numeral}, the
first three of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and the last of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}.
They are fields of the numeral's value, not static parameters of its type:
the three numeral types have no static parameters.
So \EXP{3.125} is a \TYP{RadixPointNumeral} whose four numbers are $4$, $3$,
$10$ and $3125$, and \EXP{007} a \TYP{NaturalNumeral} whose four numbers are
$3$, $0$, $10$ and $7$.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

The radix of a numeral is ten, unless its digits are followed by an underscore
and a radix indicator (\secref{numerals}), which give its radix $r$; such a
numeral has the same type as one without an indicator.
So \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16}} is a \TYP{NaturalNumeral} whose four numbers are
$5$, $0$, $16$ and $912092$.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave a numeral
the types \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket} for a numeral without leading zeros,
and \EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}, whose static arguments are
the four numbers.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that the four numbers are fields of the
numeral's value: the two types with an explicit radix fold into the radix, and
\TYP{Literal} into the digit count, which tells whether a numeral has leading
zeros.
So the team's draft notes above are answered: two numerals of one kind have one
type, which holds every such numeral, and \TYP{Numeral} comprises the two
numeral types.}


A numeral is converted where it stands, into the type that its place fixes,
and not before, because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect numerals to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it to a floating-point number before its place is known
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used where a floating-point interval is expected,
it is better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, each of the eight number types (\secref{basic-rationals}) declares
a coercion from \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} declare one from \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}; the conversion
is exact into the five integer types (\secref{basic-integers}) and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and rounds once, to the nearest value of the type, into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}.

A place \emph{fixes a type} for a numeral when the type declared there declares
a coercion from the numeral's type, as each number type of \library\ does and a
type of a program's own may, or is a numeral type itself.
The declared type of a variable, a field or a parameter, and the declared
return type of a functional, are such places, the parameter types of the
declaration that a call invokes among them (\secref{resolving-coercion}).
There the numeral is converted into that type, from its exact value:
so \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.1} binds the rational \EXP{1/10},
\EXP{r\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.1} the floating-point number nearest to it, and
\EXP{n\COLON\mathbb{N}32 = 5} the natural number 5.
It is a static error if the numeral's value lies outside the range of that
type, or rounds to an infinity there.
Where nothing fixes a type, as where a variable is declared without a type, or
a parameter has the type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number} or a type
parameter declared without a bound, the numeral is converted into its
\emph{default}: a numeral without a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or into
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds \VAR{x} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\VAR{bigN} = 3000000000} binds \VAR{bigN} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{y = 0.5} binds \VAR{y} as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64};
\EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3};
and for \EXP{\KWD{object}\;\TYP{Cell}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)},
\EXP{\TYP{Cell}(3)} is a \EXP{\TYP{Cell}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}.
\secref{numeral-default} says where else a numeral takes its default, as where
several numerals fix one type parameter, and how a numeral whose conversions
tie is read.
The default applies to a numeral, and to a static expression of numerals once
it is folded (\secref{static-expr}), never to an expression of a numeral type.

A type of a program's own receives a numeral through its own coercion from the
numeral's type, such as \EXP{\KWD{coerce}(x\COLON\TYP{RadixPointNumeral})},
whose body reads the four numbers.
A numeral at a place whose type is a type of a program's own that declares no
coercion from the numeral's type is a static error: coercion does not chain
(\secref{coercion}), so the numeral is not converted into its default first.
The coercion sees the four numbers of a numeral as written: a negative constant
reaches it as the prefix operator \EXP{-} applied to the coercion's result for
the natural numeral (\secref{static-expr}), so a type without that operator
refuses it.
At each place where such a numeral stands, the coercion is applied once, not at
each evaluation of the place, so that the numeral there denotes one object, as
a string literal does: two evaluations of one place yield the same object, and
each place has its own application of the coercion.
A numeral type is written in a program only as the type of a parameter, of a
coercion or of an operator, never as the type of a variable, a field or a
functional's result, nor as a static argument; so the constants \VAR{pi} and
\VAR{e} of \library\ are values of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Inside the body of a coercion, two values of a numeral type are equal, and
strictly equivalent, when their values $v/r^m$ are equal: there \EXP{2.5} and
\EXP{2.50} are strictly equivalent, and so are \EXP{0.1_{2}} and \EXP{0.5}.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types, and so gave a
numeral where nothing fixes a type its own type.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral is converted where it
stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type, and elsewhere into the
default above; that a type of a program's own receives a numeral only through
its coercion from the numeral's type, once for each place; and that the numeral
types are written only as parameter types.
The text this replaces, the revival's own of 29~September 2026
(\secref{revival-numeral-type}), named the type of an integer numeral
\TYP{IntLiteral}, the name that the compiled path's own library gives it.}

\secref{natparams} gains a box on a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value, and
the binary chapter's declarations over \TYP{NaturalNumeral} gain eight boxes;
the text of both stands.
The entries \secref{revival-numeral-type}, \secref{revival-inference},
\secref{revival-asfloat} and \secref{revival-object-kinds} are revised where
they named \TYP{IntLiteral} or said what the interpreter does with a numeral.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral is converted where it
stands, into the type that its place fixes or else into the machine default;
that its own type is the Working Draft's \TYP{NaturalNumeral} or
\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}, below \TYP{Numeral}, the four numbers fields of its
value; and that a type of a program's own receives a numeral through its
coercion from that type, which the compiled code applies once for each place.
The Working Draft gives numerals types of their own so that library designers
decide by coercions how numerals meet other types, and so that an interval type
receives \EXP{3.1415926535897932384} unrounded
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex}, lines
132--148).
The team built that coercion under its own names, with the numeral's exact
value, in the compiled path's own library (``ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as
described in the spec'', the team's commit \texttt{128f313b5b} of 17~November
2009, in the revival's repository), but never the four numbers.
The change keeps what the team built, one type for each kind of numeral with
its exact value at the coercion, and adds the Working Draft's names and
numbers: a coercion that receives only a floating-point value rounds twice, as a
16-bit floating-point type of a program's own would round
\EXP{1.00390625000000000001} first to the nearest \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and then to
a 16-bit value other than the one nearest to the numeral.
A field cannot give a static size, so the binary chapter's static word width
from a numeral's digit count cannot be declared, and its \EXP{\|} with a numeral
has no static result type; those declarations stand, each with a box.
The default is the type that the interpreter already gave an integer numeral by
its value, and the Java programming language's type for an integer literal.
The revival declined exact defaults, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, as
the team's restart of 2012 gives \EXP{\mathbb{N}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick},
line 25), since its model program's constants declared without a type would then
be rationals and every index declared without a type would need a conversion.
In two places the change departs from the revival's rule that the team's later
decision wins over its earlier one: the compiled path's own library, the team's
later word, names its numeral types \TYP{IntLiteral} and \TYP{FloatLiteral}, and
keeps a numeral's own type at every place that fixes no type.
The revival takes the Working Draft's names and the default as its own
finishing of the text; no source of the team calls those names either final or
temporary.
The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time, that ``IntLiterals should
always be transient objects with minimal lifetime''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java},
lines 21--23), is kept: a program meets a numeral's value only inside a
coercion or an operator whose parameter has a numeral type.
An expression of numerals alone is folded exactly, as the Working Draft computes
a static rational expression exactly and rounds it at most once
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex}, lines
162--173); its result is a signed constant written as numerals, not a value of a
constant trait, so that a coercion of a program's own sees only the four numbers
of a numeral as written, and \EXP{x = 7/2} stays a rational.
A \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value has one type, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, as the
revival decided on 28~September 2026 for the ranges (\secref{revival-inference}),
not \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} as \secref{natparams} says.
A numeral at a type of a program's own that declares no coercion from the
numeral's type is refused, since coercion does not chain; the alternative not
taken converts it into its default first and then by the type's own coercion
from that default.
A reversal to the Working Draft's polymorphic numerals would keep a numeral's
own type wherever nothing fixes a type, as the compiled path's own library does,
so that \EXP{x = 3} binds a numeral and \EXP{\TYP{Cell}(3)} is a
\EXP{\TYP{Cell}\llbracket\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\rrbracket}; a reversal to the names
of \secref{revival-numeral-type} would rename the two types \TYP{IntLiteral} and
\TYP{FloatLiteral}, which no program that does not write them would notice.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md} and
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-literals-spec/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.

type and give it its default elsewhere.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and \EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true}

refused them (row~454); a variable bound from \EXP{3000000000} is a

content.content:
Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.

- A float numeral to the left of an `RR32` operand runs `RR64`'s operator: for `a: RR32`, `2.5 + a` is an `RR64`, and `a + 2.5` an `RR32` (ledger row 958). Bind the numeral at `RR32` first, as `c: RR32 = 2.5`, then write `c + a`.
- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so its `digits` getter gives 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
- `u =/= 0` is `true` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so is `q =/= 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2` (ledger row 966). Write `NOT (u = 0)`.
- A numeral that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64` gives `Infinity`, with no error (ledger row 967).
- A negative constant, as `-3` or `5 - 8`, at a program's own number type reaches its `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` with its sign, as a natural numeral of value -3, not as `-` on the coercion of 3 (ledger row 968).
- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:

- coercion;
- chained comparisons;
- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
  - At a program's own generic type, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). Bind the value once, at a top-level variable.
  - A negative constant at a program's own number type reaches its coercion with its sign, as -3, not as `-` on the coercion of 3 (ledger row 961).
  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps the type `IntLiteral`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Give each binder a type.
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).

7:The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.
9:If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

### The scope: two rungs

- **A**, the static numerals on both paths, from the probe's patch, and what the probe did not build.
- **T**, the specification. It lands only with A.

The reasons:

1. **The probe's patch is one state, so it is one rung.** Its library alone crashes the base's checker (the count printed no total, PROBE `3. Step 2`), and its checker, code generator, prelude and walk all read that library. A rung of the library and a rung of the checker would each fail on its own tree. And the gather applies each rung's whole change from the base (`git diff BASE...<branch>`, then `git apply --3way`; the manual's "Gather", "Each rung"), so two rungs that each carried the patch would conflict wherever one of them changed the patch's lines further.
2. **What the probe did not build lies in the patch's own files**: the code generator's site machinery, the coercion desugarer and walk's numerals. No rung beside A could build on the patch without carrying it.
3. **T is prose**, builds on no code, runs beside A, and lands only with A, as climb batch 29's T landed only with the rungs whose code it described.
4. **Two rungs fit the week's limit**: about 4.2M tokens written (Cost), against climb batch 29's 7.54M for six rungs (`reviews/batch-29-review.md`, section 2).

### The point for him in the morning

**Question 1 of the probe: `u = 0` for a zero `u: NN32`, and its kin (`w = 0` for an `NN64`, `0 = u`).** With the `=` pairs between the numeral types and the number types deleted ("It was a wrong choice and it gets deleted", SNAP `11. Consequences`), `u = 0` meets two declarations: the library's `=` over `Any`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` (P-173: at `Any` a numeral takes its default), answering `u SEQV 0`, `false`; and `NN32`'s own `=`, which the numeral reaches only by its conversion. The snapshot's section 11 gives `true`, "the checker fixes `0` at `NN32` from the other operand and folds it". The tree's rule that a declaration applicable without a coercion runs before one that needs it gives `false` (P-173's `gg(5, w)` by P-49; walk's `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchForNumeralsInternal`, PROBE `13. Questions`). The ways (PROBE `13. Questions`, question 1): (a) a numeral reaches a declaration by its conversion before one it fits only at its default, where that declaration is more specific, which changes the tree's rule and walk's dispatch; (b) `false`, strict equivalence of an `NN32` and a `ZZ32`; (c) the pairs kept, against his word. **Landed, not built further:** the probe's state. Under walk `u = 0` is `false`: the eight assertions of it and its kin move into `tests/XXXNumeralEqualsNumberWalk.fss`, which asserts the snapshot's `true` and expects its failure (PROBE `7. Step 6`), with a new ledger row; on the compiled path it is `true`, since the prelude declares no `=` over `Any` (PROBE `10. What was not built`). **Consequential:** each way reads P-173 or the snapshot anew.

   - a numeral as written at a library type goes through that type's own coercion. The compiler evaluates the coercion's body over a closed set of expressions: the four numbers, constants, the fold's exact operators, and natives over the number types run at compile time. It never knows the target type. A primitive result becomes a JVM constant; anything else becomes a static final.
   - every numeral coercion is one method taking the four numbers as `ZZ` values, called once per place from any component. This is the probe's way (a).    - folded constants at a library type convert from their exact value on both paths, so no numeral coercion ever sees a sign.
   - the minus is hoisted into the static final; the compiled path's dead `IntLiteral` classes are deleted; row 957's second case is built if it fits; row 971 is not built.
